C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage sharply in rural or high-unemployment regions
C005.object: the closure rate of small businesses that rely on low-skill labor
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage sharply in rural or high-unemployment regions the closure rate of small businesses that rely on low-skill labor]

[PATH:empirical] Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) matched with state-level minimum wage changes in rural high-unemployment counties — Provides longitudinal establishment-level data on business closures and employment, allowing difference-in-differences or event-study analysis of sharp minimum wage increases in the specified geographic and temporal scope.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or administrative data from state Departments of Labor on small business survival rates, combined with local unemployment statistics and industry composition (e.g., NAICS codes for retail, accommodation, food services) — Enables direct measurement of closure rates among price-sensitive small retailers in rural counties with >8% unemployment, controlling for regional economic trends and pre-existing business density.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis or systematic review of minimum wage effects on small business survival in low-density labor markets (e.g., studies from the Upjohn Institute, NBER working papers on rural labor markets) — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence on heterogeneous effects by geography and labor market tightness, clarifying whether the hypothesized acceleration is supported or contradicted in similar contexts.

scope.domain: rural counties with high unemployment and a high density of small, price-sensitive retailers

qualifier.geographic: rural counties in the United States with unemployment rates above 8% and a high density of small, price-sensitive retailers

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage sharply
C006.object: employment opportunities for low-skilled workers in elastic labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage sharply employment opportunities for low-skilled workers in elastic labor markets]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data on county-level minimum wage changes in rural U.S. counties (e.g., from the Quarterly Workforce Indicators) matched with local employment rates for low-skilled workers — This allows direct causal estimation of employment effects in elastic labor markets where small businesses dominate, exploiting variation in minimum wage hikes across similar rural regions.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level surveys or administrative data on employee turnover and productivity in small businesses before and after a minimum wage increase — Tests the qualifier's claim that higher wages reduce turnover and boost productivity, which could offset job losses; needed to validate the proposed mechanism.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on minimum wage effects in low-elasticity labor markets (e.g., Card & Krueger 1994, subsequent replications, and newer quasi-experimental work) — Provides a synthesized view of whether sharp minimum wage increases consistently lead to employment gains in elastic settings, and under what conditions the hypothesized positive effects hold.

scope.domain: rural or high-unemployment regions with many small businesses

qualifier.context: higher wages boost worker productivity, reduce turnover, and stimulate local demand, offsetting any potential job loss

C009.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C009.object: formal-sector employment among low-skilled workers, while simultaneously increasing informal-sector participation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage formal-sector employment among low-skilled workers, while simultaneously increasing informal-sector participation]

[PATH:empirical] Micro-level panel data from household surveys (e.g., ENNIV in Peru or ENEMDU in Ecuador) covering early 2000s, with difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity analysis around minimum wage changes — Directly tests the predicted labor reallocation from formal to informal sectors within the specified geographic and temporal scope, controlling for individual fixed effects and time-varying shocks.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level surveys of low-productivity formal-sector firms in Latin America and Sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., World Bank Enterprise Surveys) coupled with linked employer-employee data — Examines whether firms respond to wage hikes by reducing formal employment, shifting workers to informal arrangements, or substituting capital, providing micro-foundational evidence for the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching models with endogenous informal sector and wage enforcement (e.g., Bosch & Esteban-Pretel, 2012, or similar extensions calibrated to developing economy data) — Tests whether the hypothesized dual effect is consistent with equilibrium conditions under weak enforcement and low productivity, and identifies conditions under which the effect intensifies or attenuates.

scope.domain: labor markets with weak enforcement of wage laws and low productivity firms

qualifier.geographic: developing economies in Latin America and Sub-Saharan Africa

C010.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C010.object: informal or underreported employment among low-skilled workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage informal or underreported employment among low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Country-level panel studies on minimum wage increases and informal employment, e.g., using ILO or national household survey data for developing countries (e.g., India, Brazil, Indonesia) during the 2010s — Directly tests the causal link between minimum wage hikes and informal/underreported employment in the specified geographic and temporal scope, controlling for enforcement strength.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level administrative data audits or tax records from weak-enforcement labor markets, comparing registered vs. unregistered workers before and after wage policy changes — Provides micro-level evidence on whether firms shift workers into informal arrangements to evade higher wage costs, addressing the exact outcome (underreported employment).

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of dual labor markets incorporating wage floors and enforcement gaps, e.g., extensions of the Harris-Todaro framework or search-and-matching models with informality — Clarifies mechanisms and conditions under which minimum wages reduce formal employment or increase informal work, guiding empirical predictions for weak-enforcement contexts.

scope.domain: labor markets with weak enforcement of wage laws

qualifier.geographic: in developing countries with weak labor law enforcement
